title: Noah Found Favour in Yahweh's Eyes — Violence, Grief, Favour
blocks: Brothers and sisters, the register we read last time was full of one phrase — "and he died" — and right in the middle of that register stood one man who walked with God for three hundred years. Today the camera pulls back from a single man to a whole generation, and we are going to come across one of the most shattering sentences in the entire Bible.

The question this lesson puts to us is this: has it ever crossed your mind that God might grieve over a generation? We are quite used to saying that God is almighty, that God is just, that God does not change. But can God hurt?

Let me put the answer up front. God does not stand there coldly watching the world rot. He hurts. And in the very same passage where his heart is breaking, he has already chosen one man, and the building of the ark has already begun. Judgement and grace have never been two separate passages of Scripture. They are one passage.
1. An Opening That Is Hard to Explain

Verses 1 to 4: "When men began to multiply on the surface of the ground, and daughters were born to them, God's sons saw that men's daughters were beautiful, and they took any that they wanted for themselves as wives."

"God's sons", בְּנֵי־הָאֱלֹהִים (benei-ha'Elohim), is the most disputed phrase in the whole chapter. Down the centuries there have been three main readings. The first takes them to be fallen angels, because "the sons of God" in Job 1:6, in 2:1 and in 38:7 all refer to angels. The second takes them to be the godly descendants of Seth, because chapters 4 and 5 have just finished separating two lines. The third takes them to be the kings and the powerful men of that age, because in the ancient Near East a king was called the son of a god, and "they took any that they wanted" carries the tone of seizing.

The position of these notes is this: we do not hand down a verdict on who they were, because all three readings point to the same one thing — a boundary was crossed. And I want you to notice the wording of the text. "Saw … were beautiful", וַיִּרְאוּ… כִּי טֹבֹת, is the same set of words used in Genesis 3:6 of Eve, who "saw that the tree was good for food"; and "they took", וַיִּקְחוּ, is the very same verb as Eve's "she took some of its fruit". The author is saying: here it is again — they saw, and they took.

Brothers and sisters, I want to say something here especially to every co-worker who stands behind a pulpit: whatever you do, never let this passage swallow the whole sermon. I have sat through far too many meetings where a solid hour went on arguing about who "God's sons" were — and the congregation walked out remembering the argument, not verse 8, "But Noah found favor in Yahweh's eyes." By all means preach the dispute. Just keep it in the proportion it deserves.

In verse 3 God says, "My Spirit will not strive with man forever, because he also is flesh; so his days will be one hundred twenty years." There are two main ways of understanding that sentence. One takes it that the human lifespan is capped from here on at a hundred and twenty years — and Moses, as it happens, lived to exactly that age. The other takes it as the countdown to the flood, a period of grace granted to that generation. These notes lean towards the second, because the context is precisely an announcement of judgement. And 1 Peter 3:20 says that God "waited patiently" in the days when Noah was building the ship — a hundred and twenty years. God is not slow to react. God is giving time.
Who exactly are "God's sons" and "men's daughters"? Does this passage have to be settled before you can preach it?

This is one of the famous cruxes of the Old Testament, and there are three main readings. The first is fallen angels — Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 are regularly brought in to support it. The second is that the godly descendants of Seth intermarried with the descendants of Cain. The third is that the kings and rulers of that age abused their power in taking wives. Honourable interpreters have argued for each of the three, and the text itself hands down no verdict. What these notes do is this: lay all three readings out, and then put the weight where the text plainly puts it — on verse 5, "Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man's heart was continually only evil." In the pulpit, say that what is uncertain is uncertain. That is not weakness; it is honesty. What is dangerous is preaching an uncertain thing as though it were settled.
2. It Grieved Him in His Heart
Verse 5: "Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man's heart was continually only evil."

Look at that verb — "saw", וַיַּרְא (vayar). In chapter 1 this word turns up more than a dozen times, and every single time the thing that follows it is "it was good." By the fifth verse of chapter 6, what God sees is "only evil." The same pair of eyes, the same action — and what they take in has been turned completely the other way round.

And "the thoughts" is יֵצֶר (yetser), whose root is the very same verb used in Genesis 2:7 when God "formed" the man. Brothers and sisters, that contrast is sharp: God formed a man, and the man formed evil. One root, two products.
Then comes verse 6, one of the most shattering sentences in the whole Bible: "Yahweh was sorry that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him in his heart."

That word "grieved" is עָצַב (atsav), and it has appeared once before, in Genesis 3:16 — "I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth." The same word. Brothers and sisters, this is the first time in the whole Bible that God's feeling is described, and the first feeling described is pain.

So let me put a question to you. Has it ever occurred to you that your sin is not merely a breach of the rules — that it can hurt the heart of a God who loves you? Ephesians 4:30 says, "Don't grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption." A great many people keep away from sin because they are afraid God will be angry. But this verse offers a far deeper motive: not fear that he will be furious, but an unwillingness to cause him pain. The lives those two motives grow are nothing like each other.
If God can be "sorry", does that mean he can also get a judgement wrong?

The Hebrew נָחַם (nacham) means to feel pain deeply, not to discover that you have miscalculated. The same word is elsewhere translated "comfort", because what it describes is the turning over of the inward parts. And Numbers 23:19 puts it perfectly plainly: "God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should repent." Scripture says both that God does not repent and that God was sorry, and there is no contradiction — the first speaks of his plans and his promises, which do not change; the second speaks of his real response to what human beings do. So this verse is not saying that God misread the situation. It is saying that God can be hurt. And a God who cannot be hurt is also a God who would never die for anyone.
If God's heart was grieved, does that mean I am supposed to go on being sad about the evil in the world forever?

Feel it — but do not stop inside the feeling. Verse 6 says that it "grieved him in his heart"; verse 8, immediately after, says, "But Noah found favor in Yahweh's eyes." The order in the text is that after the grief the work still goes on. So the healthy shape looks like this: let yourself be sad for this world, but carry that sadness into prayer, and then do the one thing that is actually within reach of your hand. Soaking in bad news for months on end and doing nothing grinds a person into one of two shapes — numbness, or contempt for the world. A practical suggestion: put a limit on how long you look at bad news each day, and make it a rule that every time you see something that grieves you, you pray for one specific person, or do one specific small thing.
3. A Light from the Original: "Sorry" Is Not God Admitting He Got It Wrong
This word "sorry" has to be made clear, or a great deal will go wrong.

In Hebrew it is נָחַם (nacham). At its core the word means to feel deeply, to sigh from the depths, to turn. It can be rendered "to be sorry", and it can just as properly be rendered "to comfort" — the "comfort" attached to Noah's name in the last lesson comes from this very root.

And then a problem arrives. Numbers 23:19 says in so many words, "God is not a man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should repent"; and 1 Samuel 15:29 says, "Also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent; for he is not a man, that he should repent." Is that not a flat contradiction?

Brothers and sisters, it is not. The key lies here: what those verses deny is that God could misjudge, that God could regret a decision of his own. What Genesis 6:6 describes is God's real and deep pain over what human beings have done. God did not get his sums wrong. God's heart was broken.

Let me put it in a picture. A father raises his son, puts him through school, gives him everything he has. The son grows up and takes a wrong road. And the father says, "I should never have …" — do you understand what that sentence means? He is not saying he is sorry the boy was ever born. That is the voice of a father whose heart is breaking. When God says, "I am sorry that I have made them", the tone is exactly the same.

So this verse does not make God smaller. It makes him alive. He is not a cold adjudicating machine; he is a God with a heart. And precisely because he has a heart, his judgement is not an arbitrary outburst — it is a decision reached on the far side of grief.
What does "violence" (חָמָס) refer to? Is it the same as what we mean by violence today?

Its range is wider than we imagine. In the Old Testament חָמָס means the injustice of the strong against the weak — it takes in violence, and it also takes in oppression, exploitation, false witness, and taking away what somebody else was owed. So when verse 11 says, "The earth was corrupt before God, and the earth was filled with violence", it is not talking only about killing and beating. It is talking about the whole order of a society gone bad: the strong may help themselves to whatever the weak have, and nobody calls a halt. The practical meaning of that for us is this — do not treat "I never laid a hand on anyone" as your standard of innocence. The question the text asks is: within the reach of your own power, is there anyone from whom a little more has been taken — by you, or by the system — simply because he is weaker than you?
Verse 8 is the hinge of the whole chapter: "But Noah found favor in Yahweh's eyes."

That word "favour", חֵן (chen), is here for the first time in the Bible. And I want you to notice where it appears — after the announcement of judgement, in the verse immediately following "I will destroy man whom I have created from the surface of the ground—man, along with animals …" Brothers and sisters, the first time grace steps onto the stage, it stands right beside the announcement of a flood.
Only then, in verse 9, does the text say, "Noah was a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time. Noah walked with God."

Get the order clear. Verse 8 says he found favour first; verse 9 calls him a righteous man second. It is not that he was good enough first and God then gave him grace; grace came to him first, and the righteousness that was lived out came after. That order has never once changed anywhere in the Bible. Ephesians 2:8–10 says it most clearly of all: "for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast" — and then verse 10 goes on, "For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them."

And notice those three words, "walked with God." Enoch in the last lesson is described with the same expression. Brothers and sisters, in a generation where "every imagination of the thoughts of man's heart was continually only evil", there was still somebody walking along with God. A bad environment is not a reason why you cannot walk with him.

Then from verse 13 onwards God hands him the specification for the ark: what timber, how long, how wide, how high, how many decks, where the door goes, how high to finish the roof. And verse 22 says, "Thus Noah did. He did all that God commanded him." One line of comment, six words: he did all that God commanded.

And there is one more very important word, in verse 18: "But I will establish my covenant with you." בְּרִית (berit), covenant. This is the first time the word appears in the Bible. Brothers and sisters, look carefully at that order: judgement is on its way, and God speaks about a covenant first. God does not destroy and then work out how to clear up afterwards. He makes a covenant, and then he acts.
"Noah found favor in Yahweh's eyes" — was that because he was good, or because God chose him?

The order in the text matters a great deal. Verse 8 says he "found favor" first; only in verse 9 is he called "a righteous man, blameless among the people of his time." Favour first, righteousness after. This is the Bible's consistent order, and the New Testament says it even more plainly: "for by grace you have been saved through faith … not of works." And that word "blameless" (תָּמִים) means whole, without defect — it does not mean sinless; by chapter 9 the man has drunk himself under the table. So the right reading is this: Noah was not chosen because he was good enough; he lived differently because he had been shown favour. And that is an intensely practical point. If you are walking the right road today, it is not to your credit. Somebody held you up first.
If God was going to destroy the whole earth anyway, why have Noah spend a hundred years building an ark?

1 Peter 3:20 says that God "waited patiently", and 2 Peter 2:5 calls Noah "a preacher of righteousness." Which is to say: those hundred years were not only a construction project, they were a public warning. A man building a boat on dry ground is itself a sermon that goes on being preached for a hundred years. And the specification of the ark was given by God, and the door was shut by God — the design of salvation, its timetable, the moment the door closes, all of it is in God's hands. That carries two things for us. One: God's judgement is never a sudden change of face; he always gives time first. Two: the fruit of preaching the gospel is not in our hands. Our part is to build that boat exactly as he said, even if for a hundred years not one person comes aboard.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching "God was sorry" as though God can get things wrong. We have already dealt with this. If you preach it as a misjudgement, the congregation's impression of God becomes: unreliable — and then what about the things he promised me, might he go back on those one day as well? It has to be said clearly: that is grief, not a misjudgement.

The second is spending a whole sermon arguing about who "God's sons" were. There really are several ways of taking that passage, and study notes ought to set the positions out and then give a judgement — but it should not fill up the pulpit. The real centre of gravity in this chapter is corruption, grief, favour and the ark.

The third is preaching Noah as having been chosen because he was good enough. The favour of verse 8 comes before the righteous man of verse 9. Turn that order round and you have turned grace into a reward. And one reminder: in chapter 9, the moment he comes out of the ark, he drinks himself senseless. The Bible has not written him up as a perfect man.

The fourth is frightening the congregation with the flood and never giving them the ark. The announcement of judgement and the dimensions of the ark are written in the same passage; preach the one without the other and you have quoted half a text. The effect of a sermon ought to be patience and hope, not panic. When the congregation leaves, they should love the Lord more, not fear the world more.

The fifth is turning the details of the ark into a lecture in engineering. The dimensions can be worked out and the volume can be estimated, and all of that is interesting — but verse 20 says "two of every sort will come to you": the one who brings the animals is God, not Noah. Noah is responsible for building; God is responsible for bringing. Put the weight on human engineering skill and you will miss that line.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: I am the only Christian in my workplace and the only Christian in my extended family; I disagree with the way everything around me is done — but what can one person possibly do? Brothers and sisters, this chapter was written for you. What Noah faced was not a group of people who were a bit unspiritual; it was a whole generation in which "every imagination of the thoughts of man's heart was continually only evil." And the text passes exactly one comment on him: he did all that God commanded. Notice this — God did not tell him to go and change that generation. God told him to build an ark; that is, to finish the one thing God had put into his hands. The most practical responsibility of one person inside a corrupt environment is not to turn the whole situation round. It is to hold on to the one thing God has entrusted to you. And I want to remind you of something: in a hundred and twenty years, not one person came aboard. 2 Peter 2:5 calls him "a preacher of righteousness" — he spoke, and nobody listened. So please do not measure your own faithfulness by results.

The second question: my elders say, "There are gods three feet above your head — heaven is watching what people do." Is that the same God as the God of chapter 6? My answer is that half of it is the same, and the half that is not the same is precisely the gospel. What is the same is this: the God of this chapter really is watching, and he sees very clearly. What is different is that "heaven is watching" usually carries the picture of something cold, something keeping accounts, something ready at any moment to send down disaster — whereas Genesis 6:6 says that this God who is watching is grieved in his heart. Brothers and sisters, those are two utterly different pictures of God. A God who keeps accounts is a God you will only be afraid of; a God who can be hurt is a God you will actually turn back to. So when you talk with your elders, you might put it this way: you are right, heaven really is watching; it is only that I found out later that the One who is watching feels pain while he watches — because he is a Father, not a security camera.
The environment around me is very bad and I often feel I cannot hold out. Should I leave?

First, separate two things. One: if this environment is pushing you into sin, or damaging your conscience or your physical and mental safety, then leaving has to be considered — and it should be done properly and safely. Two: if this environment merely makes you uncomfortable and very lonely, then the question to ask is, "Is there a piece of ground here that God has given me?" Noah was inside that generation filled with violence, and he did not move away; he built a boat. And what made it possible for him to hold out for a hundred years is that line in verse 9: "Noah walked with God." The people who hold out in lonely places are usually not the ones with the strongest will; they are the ones who have company. So the first step is not to decide whether to stay or go. The first step is to get the walking-together back — to find your one "2".
7. Living 321 Out — Favour Comes First, the Work Comes After
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — verse 9 says "Noah walked with God", the same expression that was used of Enoch. And the Lord Jesus lived his whole life doing what the Father showed him. My example is very concrete: do not watch how the people around me are living; watch what the One who walks with me says. In an environment where everybody is taking short cuts, that sentence will cost you a very great deal.

The Bible is my standard — God gave the length, the width and the height of the ark, the material, the number of decks, the door and the window, and Noah altered not one of them. Brothers and sisters, that is what a standard means: where God has already spoken clearly, you do not add an opinion of your own. The place where we most often come unstuck is not the grey areas the Bible says nothing about. It is the places where the Bible is perfectly clear and we would rather adjust it a little.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — verse 3 says, "My Spirit will not strive with man forever." Read that the other way round and it is a very serious warning: the Spirit of God can be refused by a human being. Acts 7:51 says, "you always resist the Holy Spirit!" Guidance is not automatic. It requires a willing heart.

Let Jesus be King — a hundred and twenty years, building a great boat on dry ground, laughed at for a hundred and twenty years. The truest test of letting Jesus be King is very often not one heroic decision; it is going on doing what he said through all the days when nobody understands and there is nothing to show for it.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — look at the subject of verse 8: "But Noah found favor in Yahweh's eyes." It is not that Noah won the favour; it is that the favour came to Noah. A person who understands that he has been shown favour has nothing left to boast about.

Establish God's system — "But I will establish my covenant with you" in verse 18 is the first appearance of the word "covenant" in the Bible. Brothers and sisters, God's system always begins from a covenant relationship; it never begins from a set of arrangements. That small group you want to build, that team, that home — if it has rules and no covenant, it will not come through the storm.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We often say, "Change begins with me", and that is true — but this chapter adds a very important limit to it. Noah changed himself, and he did not change that generation. The text records that outcome honestly. So "change begins with me" means "I change first"; it does not mean "once I have changed, the world will change along with me." If we take the second of those as a promise, then the moment the environment fails to improve, brothers and sisters will conclude that they were not spiritual enough. Faithfulness and results have to be reckoned on two separate accounts.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Sentence: "But Noah Found Favour"
Brothers and sisters, one and the same sentence sounds completely different when it falls into four different hearts.

The proud heart hears: "I am the Noah of this generation." This heart finishes chapter 6 with one overwhelming impression — that it is not like other people — and then starts putting everyone around it under a spiritual microscope. Brothers and sisters, see this clearly: Noah did not find favour because he was better; he was called righteous because he had found favour. And after he came out of the ark, he drank himself under the table. Chapter 6 is not a permit to feel superior.

The fearful heart hears: "The flood is nearly here — will I be in time?" This heart starts to feel anxious the moment judgement is mentioned, and cannot sleep at the news of a disaster, an epidemic, a war. To a heart like that I want to say: notice who shut the door of the ark. Genesis 7:16 says, "then Yahweh shut him in." God closed the door; Noah was not the one holding it. Your safety does not rest on how tightly you are gripping.

The ashamed heart hears: "Somebody like me could never be singled out by God." Brothers and sisters, the words "found favor" were written for you. The definition of grace is that it is given to people who do not deserve it. And notice this: at the moment Noah found favour, the text has not yet said that he was a righteous man — that comes in the next verse. You do not have to become good first in order to qualify to be loved.

The wounded heart hears: "If God was in that much pain, why did he not step in sooner?" This heart may be wrestling right now with a hurt that has gone unanswered for a very long time. I am not going to hand you a cheap answer. I only want you to look at verse 6: God hurts too. You are not weeping in front of a God who is unmoved. And 2 Peter 3:9 says that his patience is because he is "not wishing that anyone should perish, but that all should come to repentance" — that waiting which looks so much like delay may be, for someone you love, the very reason he still has a chance.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, read Genesis 6:5–8 once through, then stop and pray for one person or one situation that is causing you pain. Use a sentence like this: "Lord, this hurts you too." Put your pain and his pain side by side.

Second, find the one thing God has already told you to do that you have still not started. It does not have to be a large thing; it may be a phone call, an apology, a habit that has to stop. Noah's greatness was not in how much he understood. It was that "he did all that God commanded him."

Third, practise not measuring faithfulness by results. When this week comes to an end, do not ask, "What did I achieve?" Ask instead, "Did I do what he said?" Those two questions grow two completely different hearts.
Fourth, pray for one person who has "not yet come aboard" — pray for him by name, for seven days. God gave that generation a hundred and twenty years; you can at least give that person seven days.

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church, in three sentences: there is a line in the Bible saying that when God saw the evil of human beings, "it grieved him in his heart" — so it turns out God is not a bystander looking on coldly, he hurts; and in that very same passage he has already begun preparing a way out; so when the Bible speaks about judgement, it never leaves people without a door.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that my sin is not merely a breach of the rules — it causes my God pain; and so I will no longer treat it lightly.
I declare that I was shown favour first and called righteous after; I have nothing to boast about.
I declare that where God has already spoken clearly, I will not add an opinion of my own.
I declare that I will do what he has commanded, and will not measure my faithfulness by results.
This week I am to "really grieve once over somebody's corruption" — will that not turn into judging him?

The way to tell them apart is direction: judging pushes a person away; grief puts him into your prayers. In verse 6 God is grieved in his heart, in verse 7 he says he will destroy, and in verse 8 he still leaves an opening — there is action inside his grief. In practice there are three tests. First: have you actually said this to God, or only to other people? Second: are you grieved because he has hurt somebody, or because he has made you look bad? Third: have you ever asked for something concretely good for him? Pass all three and it is most likely real heartache. Fail one of them, and stop there: take the matter back into prayer before you say anything more.
Brothers and sisters, if only one contrast may be left over from this lesson, I want it to be verse 6 and verse 8.
Verse 6 says, "Yahweh was sorry that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him in his heart." Verse 8 says, "But Noah found favor in Yahweh's eyes."
There is one verse between them. God's heartbreak and God's grace are two lines on the same page.

Brothers and sisters, this is what the whole Bible looks like. You will not find one passage in Scripture with judgement in it and no way out. Beside the announcement of the flood, the dimensions of the ark are always laid; beside the thunder on Sinai, the pattern of the tabernacle is always laid; beside the darkness of Golgotha, that sentence is always laid — "Father, forgive them."

And Hebrews 11:7 says, "By faith Noah, being warned about things not yet seen, moved with godly fear, prepared a ship for the saving of his house, through which he condemned the world and became heir of the righteousness which is according to faith." Notice the phrase at the end: for the saving of his house. While he was building it, he probably never once imagined that the boat people had laughed at for a hundred and twenty years would in the end carry inside it his wife, his three sons and his three daughters-in-law.
The thing you are doing today that nobody around you understands may be preparing a door for your own family.

The focus is not on whether I look like Noah, not on how bad this generation is, and not on how much one person can change. The focus is on Jesus — he is that ark, and he is the Lord who was in pain for us and then died for us. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us this week: inside a generation that has gone crooked, to do everything he has commanded, and to alter not one thing. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at an idea.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; when time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear conviction.
1. ★★ The word behind "sorry" means to feel pain deeply. If you read verse 6 as "God's heart broke" rather than "God got his sums wrong", how does that change your impression of this chapter?
2. ★★★ "Violence" (חָמָס) means the injustice of the strong against the weak, not only killing and beating. Look at society today with that definition in your hand — what comes to mind?
3. ★ The order of the text is to say "found favor" first and "a righteous man, blameless" second. If that order were reversed, what would the faith turn into?
4. ★★ God "waited patiently" through the hundred years the ark was being built. What does that say to you about the way you look at the family members who have not yet believed?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, hearing, thinking, saying and walking, to digest the idea until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (at least I am not like them), fearful (the world keeps getting worse, what do we do), ashamed (I am in it too, I have no right to speak), wounded (I was hurt by that broken environment). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "But Noah found favor in Yahweh's eyes." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?

7. ★★ Is there something you went along with, even though you could plainly see it was wrong, because "everybody does it"? You do not have to give the details. Only say this: what was the excuse in your head at the time?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "The thing about this world that grieves me most is …"
9. ★★ This week, what one concrete small action will you take about the thing that grieves you? Say the time, the place and the person.

Leader's reminder: question seven will touch shame. Do not require anyone to give details, and do not let the group press one another for them. If someone speaks about injustice at work and becomes emotional, follow up with him privately after the meeting; and if anything illegal or unsafe is involved, help him take it to the proper channels.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ "Within the reach of your own power, is there anyone from whom a little more has been taken simply because he is weaker than you?" — think that question through honestly about your own home.
11. ★ The same question in another setting: what about at your workplace, or at your school?
